edges.effect_quant: Monthly skin self-examination interventions reliably increase self-check behavior, and observational data suggest earlier recognition of thinner melanomas in some settings, but direct evidence that routine monthly self-examination improves hard melanoma outcomes remains limited and partly confounded by surveillance intensity.
edges.population: adults in the general population or melanoma-survivor settings performing regular monthly skin self-examination
edges.mechanism: Repeated self-inspection can identify new or changing pigmented lesions earlier, prompting clinician assessment before lesions thicken, but it can also raise biopsy and procedure volume without clearly proving mortality benefit.
edges.summary: The evidence supports improved self-examination behavior and some stage-shift signals, but not a clean, trial-proven reduction in clinically important melanoma outcomes. A mixed label is the most faithful representation of the current literature.
edges.caveats: Many studies measure self-examination frequency rather than cancer endpoints. Observational studies are vulnerable to recall bias, healthy-user effects, and confounding from concurrent clinician skin checks.

evidence.citation: Rodgers M et al 2019 Br J Dermatol
evidence.notes: Effectiveness of interventions to support the early detection of skin cancer through skin self-examination: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
